name: Root and tuber vegetables
anchor: Per-produce-class sovereign maximum levels for lead and cadmium (EU Reg. 2023/915 and Switzerland VHK 817.022.15; Hong Kong Cap. 132V Part 2; AU-NZ Schedule 19; MERCOSUR GMC Res. 12/2011 and Paraguay Decreto 1335/2019; Israel MOH FCS-2016), nickel under EU Reg. 2024/1987, total and inorganic arsenic under MERCOSUR and Israel MOH FCS-2016, and total mercury under Hong Kong Cap. 132V and Israel MOH FCS-2016.
native_basis_label: fresh or frozen root or tuber vegetable as sold, wet weight, edible portion after washing and edible-part separation, potatoes as peeled
scope_note: Fresh and frozen roots and tubers: potato (assessed peeled, as every instrument specifies), sweet potato, carrot, parsnip, beetroot, radish, turnip, swede, celeriac, salsify, parsley root, horseradish, and the tropical roots and tubers (cassava, taro, yam, arrowroot). Frozen and pre-cut forms share the fresh wet-weight basis. This row is a distinct subcategory because roots and tubers take cadmium up from soil differently from leaves and fruits, which is the boundary rule the taxonomy states. OUT OF SCOPE: ginger and turmeric, which the Swiss root-and-tuber lead row expressly excludes and which route to Category 34 as rhizome spices; root-vegetable crisps and chips, which route to Category 7 as a snack form; dried and powdered roots (Category 34); pickled roots such as beetroot and radish (pickled-fermented-vegetables row); root vegetable juices (Category 5); single-ingredient root vegetables marketed for children under 2, which route to Category 1 and carry the FDA 20 ug/kg lead action level there rather than here; canned roots in tinplate (Category 7). COLLAPSED SOVEREIGN SPLIT: Switzerland sets cadmium at 50 ug/kg for tropical roots and tubers and for parsley roots, 100 ug/kg for temperate roots and tubers generally, 150 ug/kg for celeriac and 200 ug/kg for salsify, and its lead row excludes salsify (300 ug/kg). EU Reg. 2023/915, AU-NZ, Hong Kong, MERCOSUR and Israel each set a single 100 ug/kg cadmium value for the whole class. The row binds 50 ug/kg, so potato, carrot and beetroot certify against the value written for the cleaner tropical roots. That is over-compliance rather than a defect, but the split is worth making in the taxonomy and is recorded as an outstanding item.
basis_guard: wet weight|portion ordinarily consumed|as listed|product as offered to consumer|product as placed on market|as sold|as_sold|as consumed|commodity|edible part
basis_guard_note: Every named anchor for this row must sit in a dietary as-sold, wet-weight, edible-part or portion-ordinarily-consumed basis. The guard rejects the register's article and material bases (toy and food-contact migration, textile and leather extraction, fertiliser and growing-media dry matter, colour-additive ingredient specifications, animal-feed 12 percent moisture), any one of which would be a basis conflation if it anchored a food row.
method: HMTc Method v2.0 (government-limit-only; the strictest applicable sovereign maximum level for the row's product form in the row's native basis, a disclosed read-across where the exact cell is unregulated, a substantiated not-material determination, or a control; never occurrence-derived)

Pb.basis: wet weight, fresh root or tuber as sold, potatoes as peeled
Pb.label: Six independent credible regulators converge on 100 ug/kg lead for root and tuber vegetables (EU Reg. 2023/915, Switzerland VHK, Hong Kong Cap. 132V item 9, AU-NZ Schedule 19, MERCOSUR with Paraguay, Israel MOH FCS-2016 category 3.3); the Swiss salsify carve-out at 300 ug/kg is named so the split is visible.
Pb.substantiation: Unusually strong convergence: six instruments, one value, one basis. The EU and Swiss rows specify assessment after washing and edible-part separation with potatoes as peeled, which is the basis this row publishes. Single-ingredient root vegetables for children under 2 carry the stricter FDA 20 ug/kg action level, but that instrument is scoped to processed baby food and routes to Category 1 under the taxonomy age boundary rule, so it is not an anchor here.

Cd.basis: wet weight, fresh root or tuber as sold, potatoes as peeled
Cd.label: Switzerland VHK 817.022.15 sets cadmium at 50 ug/kg for tropical roots and tubers and for parsley roots, the strictest sovereign cadmium maximum level applicable to any member of this row; six instruments set 100 ug/kg for roots and tubers generally, and the Swiss celeriac and salsify carve-outs sit at 150 and 200 ug/kg.
Cd.substantiation: Cassava, taro, yam and parsley root are in this row, and 50 ug/kg is the sovereign value written for them, so it is the strictest applicable value and the method selects it. The full split (50, 100, 150, 200 ug/kg) is named so the derivation report shows exactly what a single-row taxonomy is collapsing. The consequence is disclosed: potato, carrot and beetroot are held to a value written for the cleaner tropical roots, which is twice as strict as the six-instrument consensus for those species. Occurrence data was not consulted, and no feasibility adjustment was made in either direction.

tAs.basis: wet weight, fresh root or tuber as sold
tAs.label: MERCOSUR GMC Res. 12/2011 and Paraguay Decreto 1335/2019 set total arsenic for roots and tubers at 200 ug/kg, twice the value the same instrument sets for bulb, cucurbit and leguminous vegetables; Hong Kong sets 500 ug/kg for vegetables and Israel 1000 ug/kg.
tAs.substantiation: Direct maximum level for the exact product form. MERCOSUR's own decision to set roots and tubers at 200 ug/kg while holding other vegetable classes at 100 ug/kg is a government-written product-form split and is preserved rather than overridden with the stricter value from a class this row does not contain. The inorganic-arsenic species limit of 60 ug/kg remains the operative arsenic constraint.

iAs.label: Israel MOH FCS-2016 category 3 sets the only inorganic-arsenic maximum level any credible government writes for fruits and vegetables (60 ug/kg); the EU, Codex, FDA, AU-NZ, Hong Kong and Swiss instruments set inorganic-arsenic maximum levels only for rice, juices, seaweed and infant food.
iAs.substantiation: Inorganic arsenic is the health-relevant arsenic species and is never satisfied by the total-arsenic cell; both are reported. This value is a direct maximum level for the product class, not a read-across, and it sits well below the total-arsenic ceiling for the same row, so the species cell is the binding arsenic constraint in practice.

tHg.basis: food as listed in Cap 132V Part 2 Schedule; source unit mg/kg
tHg.label: Hong Kong Cap. 132V item 12 sets total mercury for vegetables other than edible fungi at 10 ug/kg, the strictest sovereign total-mercury maximum level applicable to this product form; Israel MOH FCS-2016 category 3 sets 30 ug/kg for the same commodity class.
tHg.substantiation: Both named rows are direct maximum levels for the vegetable class in an as-sold basis. Hong Kong binds. Edible fungi are expressly outside the Hong Kong row (they carry 100 ug/kg under the same item) and route to Category 29, so the 10 ug/kg value is not being borrowed from a mushroom limit.

MeHg.rationale: No credible sovereign government sets a methylmercury maximum level for this product form: stasinos2014-heavy-metals-tubers-review measured methylmercury in this matrix, so the species is not absent and no not-material determination is supportable. Methylmercury is therefore held under mandatory analytical control rather than recorded not-material, and it remains bounded by identity below the published total-mercury ceiling for this row (methylmercury cannot exceed total mercury). No methylmercury ceiling is invented.
MeHg.reference_method: Methylmercury by GC-ICP-MS or EN 16801, required only on a lot whose total mercury reaches 60 percent of the published total-mercury ceiling; any quantifiable methylmercury on such a lot is investigated and the lot is held pending root-cause analysis.

Ni.basis: wet weight, fresh root or tuber as sold
Ni.label: EU Reg. 2024/1987 sets nickel for root, tuber and bulb vegetables at 900 ug/kg, mirrored by Switzerland VHK Wurzel- und Knollengemüse at the same value.
Ni.substantiation: Direct maximum level for the exact product form from the only comprehensive dietary nickel instrument in existence. The EU deliberately set roots, tubers and bulbs above leafy (500) and fruiting (400) vegetables, which is a government-written product-form split and is preserved; no stricter vegetable-class nickel value is applicable to a root or tuber.

Sn.rationale: Every tin maximum level in the register is scoped to canned product: EU Reg. 2023/915 sets 200000 ug/kg for canned foods and 100000 ug/kg for canned beverages, Codex CXS 193-1995 and AU-NZ Schedule 19 set 250000 ug/kg for canned foods, and Hong Kong Cap. 132V sets 250000 ug/kg for canned food other than canned beverages. Those limits regulate one contamination pathway, dissolution of tin from tinplate into the packed food. This row is not packed in tinplate, so the pathway that every sovereign tin limit addresses is physically absent and any tin present is dietary background rather than packaging migration. Fresh and frozen roots and tubers are sold loose, netted, bagged or in polymer trays. Hermetically sealed tinplate presentations of this commodity route to the canned-foods row in Category 7 and carry the canned-foods tin maximum level there.
Sn.reference_method: Total tin by ICP-MS on every lot as part of the mandatory eight-totals panel; a result above 50 ug/kg is investigated for a metal-contact source in harvest, wash, transport or packing before the lot is released.
Sn.regulatory_basis: No jurisdiction sets a tin maximum level for non-canned produce; all tin maximum levels in the register are conditioned on a canned (tinplate) presentation, and the EU rows expressly exclude canned dried and canned powdered products from even that scope.
Sn.jurisdictions_checked: EU Reg. 2023/915; EU Reg. 2024/1987 (nickel); Switzerland VHK 817.022.15 (2026 metal/metalloid annex); Hong Kong Cap. 132V Part 2 Schedule; AU-NZ Food Standards Code Schedule 19; MERCOSUR GMC Res. 12/2011 and Paraguay Decreto 1335/2019; Israel MOH FCS-2016; Codex CXS 193-1995; US FDA (21 CFR, action levels)

Al.rationale: No credible sovereign government sets an aluminium contaminant maximum level for any fruit, vegetable or produce form in any jurisdiction. The register's aluminium limits are drinking-water and bottled-water parameters, infant-formula maximum levels, a food-contact plastics specific migration limit, toy migration limits, and permitted-additive levels for baked and starch foods; none of them regulates aluminium as a contaminant of produce. Aluminium is also the third most abundant element in the earth's crust and appears in produce largely as soil-derived and root-associated mineral content rather than as process contamination, so no near-neighbour read-across is supportable either. Under the government-limit-only method HMTc publishes no standalone aluminium number for this row.
Al.reference_method: Total aluminium by ICP-MS on every lot, reported to the applicant. Document any aluminium-containing processing aid, packaging contact or anti-caking agent, comply with the additive rules of every market of sale, and investigate any result that is an outlier against the applicant's own lot history.

Cr.screen_note: Total chromium is recorded as a SCREEN, not a protective ceiling. Dietary chromium is dominated by nutritionally essential Cr(III); the health-relevant species is Cr(VI), which is controlled separately by reflex speciation. A lot may satisfy this screen and still fail on Cr(VI), and the screen is excluded from the firm-limit count.
Cr.basis: food as listed in Cap 132V Part 2 Schedule; source unit mg/kg
Cr.label: Hong Kong Cap. 132V item 7 sets total chromium for vegetables other than pulses at 500 ug/kg, the only dietary total-chromium maximum level any credible government writes for this product form.
Cr.substantiation: Named as the sovereign total-chromium value for the vegetable class in its as-sold basis. Pulses are expressly outside this row (1000 ug/kg under the same item) and route to Category 27. Total chromium never satisfies the Cr(VI) cell.

Cr-VI.rationale: No credible sovereign government sets a hexavalent-chromium maximum level for any food in any jurisdiction; every Cr(VI) limit in the register governs articles and materials (toys, textiles, leather, fertilisers, electrical equipment), not diet. Chromium in produce is dominated by nutritionally essential Cr(III), and Cr(VI) is not stable in the plant matrix: fruit and vegetable tissue is an aqueous, organic-acid and ascorbate-rich reducing medium in which Cr(VI) is reduced to Cr(III), so a reported Cr(VI) value in this matrix reflects extraction conditions rather than the chromium species the consumer ingests. Hexavalent chromium is therefore bounded by the published total-chromium screen for this row (Hong Kong Cap. 132V item 7, 500 ug/kg) and controlled by reflex speciation rather than by a published number.
Cr-VI.reference_method: Total chromium by ICP-MS on every lot. Any total-chromium result at or above 100 ug/kg triggers Cr(VI) speciation by EN 15192 or EPA 6800 IC-ICP-MS isotope dilution; any quantifiable Cr(VI) at LOQ fails the lot. Cr(VI) is never published as a panel number.
Cr-VI.regulatory_basis: No jurisdiction sets a dietary Cr(VI) maximum level; the register's Cr(VI) rows are article and material limits (EU 2009/48 toys, EU 2018/1513 textiles, EU 301/2014 leather, EU 2019/1009 fertilisers, EU RoHS). The total-chromium parent for this row is published.
Cr-VI.jurisdictions_checked: EU Reg. 2023/915; EU Reg. 2024/1987 (nickel); Switzerland VHK 817.022.15 (2026 metal/metalloid annex); Hong Kong Cap. 132V Part 2 Schedule; AU-NZ Food Standards Code Schedule 19; MERCOSUR GMC Res. 12/2011 and Paraguay Decreto 1335/2019; Israel MOH FCS-2016; Codex CXS 193-1995; US FDA (21 CFR, action levels)
